title: Sen. Cortez Masto Reintroduces Bill to Shield DACA Recipients From Deportation
excerpt: The Fairness for Immigrant Families Act would prohibit deportation of DACA recipients with pending renewals and create new pathways to citizenship, as hundreds of Dreamers face detention amid growing processing delays.
body:
• The Fairness for Immigrant Families Act would bar deportation of DACA recipients and immigrants with pending applications, while creating pathways to permanent residency for long-term residents.
  • DHS confirmed 261 DACA recipients were detained and 86 deported between January and November 2025, with renewal processing times stretching from one month to over five months.
  • The bill also targets notario fraud, requires high-level approval before deporting parents of U.S. citizen children, and mandates greater transparency in immigration fee spending.
  • Roughly 506,000 DACA recipients nationwide face risk of losing work authorization as legal challenges and processing backlogs continue to mount.

What the Bill Proposes

U.S. Senator Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) has reintroduced the Fairness for Immigrant Families Act, a sweeping immigration reform package that would prohibit the deportation of DACA recipients and immigrants with pending applications while establishing new pathways to citizenship for long-term residents.

The legislation would make it easier for long-term immigrants with clean records to become lawful permanent residents by eliminating bars to reentry and restoring the 245(i) program for those with family ties. It would require senior-level DHS approval before any parent of a U.S. citizen child is deported, and direct the State Department to establish an office for U.S. citizen children who have followed a deported parent out of the country.

"Hardworking, law-abiding immigrant families across the U.S. are looking to Congress to finally address immigration reform. While our immigration system has long been broken, I believe it can be fixed."

— Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.)

The bill also criminalizes notario fraud — schemes to provide fraudulent immigration services — creates grant programs to help states crack down on such scams, and requires DHS to report detailed financial data on immigration fee collection and adjudication backlogs.

A Response to Escalating DACA Enforcement

The legislation arrives at a critical moment. According to DHS data, 261 DACA recipients were detained between January and November 2025, with 86 deported. Separate DHS figures put the numbers higher, with 270 arrested and 174 removed during a slightly different reporting window.

Renewal processing delays have compounded the crisis. USCIS data shows median processing times ballooned from roughly one month in late 2023 to over five months. Legal aid organizations sued the Trump administration in June 2026 in the Northern District of California, demanding data on the backlog.

The human toll has been stark. Juan Sebastian Chavez Velasco was detained by ICE in February while driving to deliver milk to his newborn daughter in a hospital NICU. His renewal, submitted the previous November, remained pending — his DACA expired in March while he sat in detention. Maria de Jesús Estrada Juárez, a 42-year-old mother, was detained and deported after a green card interview before a federal judge ordered her return.

"DHS, because of their punitive deportation plan, are slow walking this intentionally so they can use this as a change of circumstance for these DACA recipients. It really is a betrayal of the system, a betrayal of a community who has faithfully trusted the United States government."

— Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, to NOTUS

Legal and Political Landscape

The bill's reintroduction comes as DACA's legal foundations erode. The Fifth Circuit found DACA's work authorization provisions unlawful in January 2025, though it suggested deportation protections could be severed from employment benefits. In April 2026, the Board of Immigration Appeals ruled that DACA status alone is insufficient reason to terminate removal proceedings — further weakening protections recipients had relied on for over a decade.

Cortez Masto has led a broader Democratic push on the issue, joining Senator Dick Durbin in leading 40 Senate Democrats to demand DHS reduce renewal delays. The bill is endorsed by UnidosUS, the ACLU, United We Dream Action, FWD.us, the American Immigration Lawyers Association, and several Nevada-based organizations.

Diaspora Implications

While the majority of DACA recipients are of Latin American origin, the bill's provisions on eliminating reentry bars and restoring adjustment-of-status pathways could benefit Indian immigrants caught in decades-long green card backlogs — a persistent issue the legislation tangentially addresses.

What Comes Next

The bill's prospects in a Republican-controlled Congress remain slim. But with 506,000 active DACA recipients and nearly 600,000 more unable to apply due to ongoing Fifth Circuit litigation, pressure on both parties continues to build. A pending district court ruling on implementing the Fifth Circuit's decision could reshape DACA's scope before any legislative fix takes effect.
